title: PoSh: Scene Graphs as Structured Rubrics for Judging Image Descriptions
one_liner: PoSh uses scene graphs (structured diagrams of objects and their relationships) to guide LLMs in grading detailed image descriptions, catching fine-grained errors that old metrics miss.
lead: Describing a painting or photograph in words is hard to grade fairly. Old metrics like CIDEr count word matches, which works for short captions but fails for long, detailed descriptions where the real errors are subtle: mixing up which object has which color, or misplacing a relation between things. PoSh fixes this by extracting a scene graph (a diagram of objects, their properties, and how they relate) from both the reference description and the model's attempt, then asks an LLM to score how well the model's version matches the reference version on each component.

problem.h2: Grading detailed descriptions is harder than it looks
paras: A standard image metric like CIDEr or SPICE works by checking if the description contains certain words or phrases. This makes sense for short captions: you describe a dog, the system checks for the word dog, because a short caption has few ways to say the same thing, so exact word match is reliable. But detailed descriptions are long and written many ways. A human might say the dog sits beside a red barn; a model might say the dog stands by a crimson building. Both are describing the same scene, but old metrics see different words and score it as wrong.

The real errors in detailed descriptions are subtle: the object is right but the color is wrong, or the relationship is backwards (the cup is on the table versus the table is under the cup). These compositional mistakes need a judge who understands structure, not word counting.

callout.html: PoSh extracts the structure of each description (what objects, properties and relations it mentions) and asks an LLM to check how well the model's structure matches the reference structure.

panels.title: 1. Reference written by expert
panels.viz_args: A dog sits beside a red barn on grass.
panels.caption: A detailed, careful description of the painting.

panels.title: 2. Model attempts description
panels.viz_args: A dog stands by a crimson building.
panels.caption: Different words, same idea—but old metrics say it is wrong.

panels.title: 3. Extract scene graph from each
panels.caption: Scene graph lists each object, its properties, and how things relate.

panels.title: 4. LLM judges each component
panels.viz_args: Dog present? Yes. Color red? Yes, crimson close. Grass? No.
panels.caption: LLM scores whether model matched reference on each part.

panels.title: 5. Aggregate into final score
panels.caption: PoSh score reflects what LLM saw, matching human judgment better.

steps.text: Parse both descriptions to find objects, their properties, and relations.
For each component, write a question: Does the generation mention this object? Is the color correct?
Ask an LLM to read both descriptions and answer each question on a 1-5 scale.
Collect LLM scores for objects, properties, relations as separate granular error scores.
Combine component scores into overall quality and localized error categories.

paras: Instead of counting words, PoSh extracts the structure of each description—the things it names, their attributes, and the relationships between them—and judges structure-to-structure, not word-to-word.

hidden.name: Component-level match score
paras: A component-level match score is how well a single element (one object, one property, one relation) from the reference description appears correctly in the model's description. For example: Does the model mention the dog? Does it say the dog is red, not blue? Does it place the dog next to the barn, not inside it?

PoSh estimates this by templating a question for each component, feeding both descriptions to an LLM, and asking the LLM to rate on a scale of 1 to 5 whether the model captured that specific component correctly. The LLM reads the descriptions and judges similarity, so it can catch paraphrases and near-misses instead of exact word matches.

heat.caption: Darker means LLM and human raters agreed it was correct; lighter means mistakes or missing parts.

reads.html: PoSh breaks the description into small pieces (objects, colors, spatial relations) and grades each piece separately, so mistakes are caught and located, not hidden in an overall number.

The granular scoring function Ψ applies to every component c in the scene graph G(d), producing a score Ψ(c) reflecting presence and correctness in the peer description. Aggregate functions then roll these component scores into mistake/omission categories.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: structured rubrics catch relational errors
paras: Traditional metrics use word bags: they count how many words from the reference appear in the model output. This breaks for long, paraphrased descriptions because the model can say the right thing in entirely different words.

PoSh uses scene graphs as rubrics. A scene graph is a strict listing of the objects in the image, their properties (like colors, sizes), and the relations between them (who is next to whom, what is inside what). By extracting this structure from both descriptions and having an LLM compare structure-to-structure, the metric captures what the model actually understood about the spatial and semantic composition of the image, not just surface word overlap.

The LLM acts as a flexible bridge: it reads two descriptions and judges whether the model's version captures the same structural facts as the reference, even if the words are completely different. This is why PoSh matches human judgment better—humans also care about compositional correctness, not word-for-word repetition.

stages.s: Parse: extract scene graphs (objects, properties, relations)
Template: write a structured question for each component
Judge: LLM reads both and scores component similarity on 1-5
Aggregate: roll up component scores into error and quality scores
Granular + coarse scores that match human judgment

math.h2: The aggregation formula: weighted component scores
math.words: Final score is the average of LLM component scores, weighted by importance. Mistakes (where model says something wrong) and omissions (where model fails to mention something) are separated and reported as distinct error types.
math.equation: PoSh_score = (sum of component scores) / (number of components), where each component score is LLM_judgment(reference_component, model_description)
symbols: One object, property, or relation from the reference scene graph
The full description generated by the model
The LLM's 1-5 score for how well the component appears in the model description

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Reference has 5 components: dog (object), red (color), barn (object), beside (relation), grass (property).
LLM scores for model description: dog=5 (present), red=3 (close: says crimson), barn=4 (present), beside=5 (correct), grass=1 (omitted).
Mistakes: color slightly wrong (LLM gave 3 instead of 5), totals 2 points of localized error.
Omissions: grass missing entirely (LLM gave 1), totals 4 points of omission cost.
Humans looking at the same generation rate it 3.7, close to PoSh's 3.6.

math.note: By grading each structural piece separately, PoSh pinpoints exactly where the model went wrong and aggregates fairly, matching how humans judge detailed descriptions.

bars.h2: How PoSh correlates with human judgment better than old metrics

charts.title: Old metric (CIDEr word-counting)
charts.note: Word-based metrics penalize paraphrases even if the description is correct; they miss fine-grained compositional errors.

charts.title: PoSh (structure-based)
charts.note: PoSh recognizes correct paraphrases and localizes compositional errors, matching human judgment in both cases.

items.html: If the dependency parser or coreference resolver makes mistakes, the scene graph is incomplete or malformed. Then the rubric has gaps or phantom components, and the LLM's judgment is based on a broken template.

items.b: LLM refuses the task or hallucinates.
items.html: An LLM prompted to score a component might disagree with human raters or invent a reason to rate high even when the model clearly failed. Calibration on a human-labeled set (like DOCENT) helps because the LLM sees examples of when to be strict and when to be lenient, so it learns the nuance, but drift persists because new images or unfamiliar compositions can trigger different judgment patterns.

A scene graph captures objects and relations but not tone, style, or fine aesthetic detail. A model that gets composition right but tone completely wrong will still score high on PoSh even if humans say it is poor.

When scene graphs are extracted cleanly, the LLM is prompted consistently, and the evaluation set is diverse (as in DOCENT), PoSh tracks human judgment far better than word-based metrics because the LLM judges structural understanding rather than word match, and catches real compositional errors because each component is scored independently so mistakes are visible and localized.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small test where you hand-write three descriptions of the same painting: (1) a detailed reference, (2) a model output that gets the spatial relations right but gets a color wrong, (3) a model output that paraphrases the reference correctly. Extract scene graphs for each. Prompt an LLM (like Qwen2.5) with templated component questions. Show that PoSh correctly ranks (1) and (3) far above (2), while an old word-metric would rank (3) low due to paraphrasing.
demo.metric_eq: Spearman correlation between PoSh scores and human ratings on a held-out validation set from DOCENT; PoSh >= 0.70, old metric <= 0.65
demo.closing: PoSh demo must show that structure-based judgment catches compositional errors invisible to word-counting, and that paraphrases are not penalized.
